reference.source: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology / Katz's Physiology of the Heart
clinicalPearls: Ventricular action potential: Phase 0 (inward Na+ via Nav1.5), Phase 1 (transient outward K+), Phase 2 (plateau: inward Ca2+ balanced by outward K+), Phase 3 (repolarization: IKr, IKs), Phase 4 (IK1, resting -90 mV)
Pacemaker cells (SA/AV node) exhibit spontaneous Phase 4 depolarization driven by the funny current (If) via HCN channels and T-type Ca2+ channels
Sympathetic beta-1 stimulation raises cAMP, steepening Phase 4 slope (positive chronotropy); vagal M2 stimulation opens IKACh, hyperpolarizing node (bradycardia)
Effective refractory period spans phases 0, 1, 2, and early 3, preventing tetanic contraction and ensuring rhythmic chamber filling
Early afterdepolarizations (EADs) occur during phase 2/3 in prolonged QT intervals, triggering polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (Torsades de pointes)
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital long QT syndrome arises from loss-of-function potassium channel mutations (LQT1 KCNQ1, LQT2 KCNH2) or gain-of-function sodium channel mutations (LQT3 SCN5A). Delayed ventricular repolarization permits reactivation of L-type calcium channels, triggering early afterdepolarizations that provoke Torsades de pointes and sudden cardiac death.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital long QT syndromes (Romano-Ward, Jervell and Lange-Nielsen)
additionalInvestigations: 12-lead electrocardiogram calculating corrected QT interval (QTc = QT / sqrt(RR))
24-hour ambulatory Holter ECG monitoring for transient arrhythmias
Electrophysiological study (EPS) with programmed electrical stimulation
